name: Kasara
tagline: Chitwan's park headquarters and its gharial nursery
meta_description: Kasara, headquarters of Chitwan National Park: the gharial breeding centre, the park museum, quiet jeep drives and how to get there from Sauraha.
summary: Kasara is the headquarters of Chitwan National Park, on the south bank of the Rapti in the middle of the park. It is best known for the gharial breeding centre, where eggs of this critically endangered crocodile are hatched and the young raised for release. Visit on a full-day jeep safari or stay nearby at Patihani.
intro: Kasara is where Chitwan National Park is run from: the park office, staff quarters, a small museum, an army post and the breeding centre that has kept the gharial alive in Nepal's rivers. It sits on the south side of the East Rapti, roughly in the middle of the park, about 35 km by road from Sauraha via Bharatpur and Patihani. Rangers and soldiers who patrol the park are based here.

Most visitors arrive on a full-day jeep drive from Sauraha, eat a packed lunch under the trees and spend an hour with the gharials before driving back by another track. Staying nearby, in the farm villages of Patihani across the river, gives you quieter mornings in the central part of the park, with fewer jeeps than the Sauraha side. Mornings on the central tracks can be wonderfully quiet.

Kasara is a good stop for families and anyone curious about how conservation actually works. The pens hold gharials from hatchlings a hand long to young adults over two metres, and staff explain how eggs are collected from sandbanks, hatched, and raised for years before release into the Narayani, Rapti and other rivers of the Terai. Allow at least an hour at the centre, and combine it with a jeep drive or a river walk to see wild crocodiles in their own habitat.

story.title: Saving the fish-eating crocodile
paras: The gharial is the oddest crocodile you will ever see: a long, thin snout lined with more than a hundred sharp teeth, built for catching fish and nothing else. Adult males grow a bulbous knob on the snout tip, shaped like a ghara, an earthen pot, which gives the animal its name. It hunts in deep, clean, fast rivers and almost never leaves the water except to bask and nest. It poses no danger to people.

In the early 1950s about 235 gharials lived in the Narayani. Dams, sand mining, fishing nets and the loss of nesting sandbanks cut that number to only 38 wild animals by 2003. The breeding centre at Kasara was set up to break the cycle: staff collect eggs from river sandbanks each spring, hatch them in safety, and rear the young for six to nine years before releasing them. Releases have continued year after year.

Survival after release is still low, and the gharial remains critically endangered across its range in Nepal and India. But the Kasara programme has kept animals in the Narayani and Rapti, and released gharials have been recorded far downstream. Nearby, a smaller centre cares for rescued turtles, another group of river animals in trouble. Many visitors find the nursery tanks, full of tiny hatchlings, the most hopeful sight of their Chitwan trip.

legend: In Hindu belief the gharial is linked with the goddess Ganga, who is shown riding a makara, a river creature often drawn with a long crocodile snout. Boatmen on the Narayani say a gharial basking on a sandbank brings good fishing, and older families along the river treated the animal with respect rather than fear, since it never attacks people.
people: Kasara itself is a park and army compound, home to rangers, nature guides and soldiers of the Nepal Army who patrol the park. Across the Rapti, the farm villages of Patihani and the wider Bharatpur area are home to Tharu families and hill settlers who grow rice, maize and mustard and work in tourism. Bote and Musahar families have long fished on these rivers.

untold.fact: About 235 gharials lived in the Narayani River in the early 1950s; by 2003 only 38 wild animals were counted, which is why eggs are now collected each year and hatched at the Kasara breeding centre.
Young gharials at the breeding centre are reared to an age of six to nine years before release, because hatchlings in the wild are easily lost to floods, predators and fishing nets.
The gharial takes its name from the ghara, a Hindustani word for an earthen pot, after the round knob that grows on the snout tip of adult males.

National park, as in Chitwan Rashtriya Nikunja

taste.name: Dhikri
taste.text: Dhikri is a Tharu rice-flour dough rolled into long shapes and steamed over a cloth, served with pickle, lentils or a meat curry. It is a must at Maghi in January. Ask at Tharu homes or homestays near Patihani, or order it in advance at your lodge.

highlights.title: Gharial breeding centre
highlights.text: Pens of every size, from hatchlings a hand long to young gharials more than two metres, show the whole rearing cycle. Staff explain how eggs are collected from Narayani sandbanks and when young animals are released.

highlights.title: Turtle rescue pens
highlights.text: Beside the gharial pens, a small turtle centre cares for rescued freshwater turtles and tortoises, many taken from traders or injured on roads, and returns them to the wild when they can survive. Visit with your guide.

highlights.title: The park museum
highlights.text: A modest museum at the headquarters displays skulls, skins and specimens of Chitwan's animals, plus displays on rhino conservation and poaching. It is a useful half hour before or after a drive. Allow about half an hour.

highlights.title: Quieter central park tracks
highlights.text: Starting from the Kasara side means fewer jeeps on the central tracks. Grasslands and small lakes here hold rhinos, gaur, sambar and sloth bear, and the forest is good for hornbills and woodpeckers. Dawn drives are best.

highlights.title: Rapti sunsets at Patihani
highlights.text: The riverbank at Patihani, across from Kasara, faces west over the Rapti. In the dry season rhinos and deer come to the far bank in the evening, without the crowds of Sauraha. Bring a warm layer in winter.

how_to_reach.text: From Bharatpur it is about 20 km to Patihani and Kasara, 40 minutes by car. From Sauraha the road route runs about 35 km via Bharatpur, 1 to 1.5 hours; full-day park jeeps also reach Kasara through the park. From Kathmandu allow 5 to 6 hours by road.
Fly from Kathmandu to Bharatpur (BHR), about 20 to 25 minutes, then drive about 40 minutes to Patihani and Kasara. Winter fog can delay morning flights; check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: There are no tourist rooms inside the Kasara headquarters. The nearest stays are in Patihani across the Rapti, where Kasara Resort offers villas and a pool on the edge of the park, a calm alternative to Sauraha. Bharatpur, about 40 minutes away, has business hotels and the airport. Many travellers simply visit Kasara on a full-day jeep safari from Sauraha and sleep there, or combine it with nights in Meghauli further west.
tips: Visit the gharial centre in the morning or late afternoon; in the heat of the day the animals lie still in the water.
Bring binoculars; the pens are large and some animals rest far from the railings.
Do not tap on fences or throw food to the gharials or turtles.
Your park entry ticket for the day usually covers the breeding centre; confirm with your guide.
Pair Kasara with a full-day jeep drive so you see wild gharials and muggers on the rivers as well as the pens.

experiences.title: Gharial breeding centre visit
experiences.summary: See the critically endangered gharial at every age, from tiny hatchlings to young adults, and learn how Chitwan's staff collect eggs from river sandbanks, raise the young and release them into the Narayani and Rapti.
body: The breeding centre sits in the shade of the headquarters compound. Concrete pools and fenced pens are arranged by age, so you walk from the nursery tanks, where hatchlings the length of a pencil swim in shallow water, to larger pools where young gharials of two metres or more bask with their thin snouts resting on the edge. Shade trees keep the area cool in the morning.

Staff and guides explain the cycle. Female gharials lay eggs in holes dug in river sandbanks in spring. Floods, predators and people destroy many nests, so teams collect eggs and incubate them here. The young are fed fish and reared for six to nine years until they are large enough to survive in the river, then released. Ask staff how many eggs were collected this season.

Mugger crocodiles, the broader-snouted crocodile of lakes and slow water, are kept nearby for comparison, and a small turtle centre cares for rescued species. Take time to read the boards on gharial biology and threats. The visit makes the river trips you take afterwards much richer, because you know what you are looking for. Allow about an hour, and visit before midday.

faqs.q: Is the gharial breeding centre worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes. It is one of the few places in the world to see gharials at close range, at every age from hatchling to young adult, and to understand the work that keeps them alive in Nepal. Allow about an hour. It works best as part of a full-day jeep safari from Sauraha or a stay at Patihani.

faqs.q: How do I get to the gharial breeding centre from Sauraha?
faqs.a: The usual way is a full-day jeep safari through the park from Sauraha, which stops at Kasara for lunch and the breeding centre. You can also drive by road via Bharatpur and Patihani, about 35 km and 1 to 1.5 hours. Ask your lodge which option suits the season.

faqs.q: Are gharials dangerous to people?
faqs.a: Gharials are not considered a danger to people. Their long, thin jaws are built to catch fish and cannot handle large prey. Mugger crocodiles, which share the same rivers, can be dangerous, so keep away from the water's edge and follow your guide's advice on riverbanks and in canoes.

experiences.title: Jeep drive in the park's quieter centre
experiences.summary: Starting from the Kasara side, jeeps explore the central grasslands, lakes and sal forest with fewer vehicles than the Sauraha tracks. Good odds for rhino, gaur and sambar, and a fair chance of sloth bear.
body: Lodges at Patihani run drives into the central part of the park, crossing near Kasara and heading into grassland and sal forest. Fewer jeeps use these tracks, so animals are often calmer and you can sit for longer at a lake edge or a clearing without another vehicle pulling up behind. Expect a cold, misty start in December and January.

Gaur, the world's largest wild cattle, spend much of the year in the Churia hills to the south and come down to the grasslands in spring when new grass sprouts after the fires. Chitwan's gaur population roughly doubled between 1997 and 2016, and February to April is the best time to see a herd. Watch for them in open areas near the forest edge.

Expect rhinos in the wet grassland, spotted deer in large herds, sambar near water, and many birds of prey. Sloth bears are seen on some early drives, often digging at termite mounds. Bring a jacket for the cold start in winter and a hat for the ride back. Drives last four to five hours; bring snacks and water.

faqs.q: Is the Kasara side of Chitwan better than Sauraha for wildlife?
faqs.a: Not better in species, but usually quieter. The central tracks around Kasara see fewer jeeps than the routes nearest Sauraha, so animals are often more relaxed and you share sightings with fewer vehicles. The wildlife is the same park population; skilled guides and early starts matter more than which side you enter from.

faqs.q: When are gaur easiest to see in Chitwan?
faqs.a: From about February to April. After the dry-season fires, fresh grass sprouts on the floodplain and gaur come down from the Churia hills to graze and browse in the grasslands and riverine forest. For most of the year they stay in the less accessible hills in the south of the park.

faqs.q: Can I book a private jeep from Patihani?
faqs.a: Yes. Lodges at Patihani, including Kasara Resort, arrange private jeeps with licensed nature guides and park permits. Book the evening before so permits are ready. Rates are higher than shared jeeps from Sauraha but you control the start time and pace.

experiences.title: Birding walk on the Rapti riverbank
experiences.summary: An easy guided walk along the Rapti near Patihani for kingfishers, storks, eagles, river lapwings and winter ducks, with mugger crocodiles on the sandbanks and the chance of rhinos on the far shore. Mornings are best.
body: The Rapti riverbank opposite Kasara is open and flat, which makes it ideal for an easy morning walk with a bird guide. In winter the river is low and braided, with gravel bars and sandbanks where waders feed and crocodiles bask once the sun warms the air. Walks are flat and easy, on sand, gravel and grass.

Common sightings include pied, white-throated and stork-billed kingfishers, river lapwings, great cormorants, woolly-necked and black storks, and ruddy shelducks in winter. Pallas's fish-eagle, ospreys and several other raptors hunt the river. Chitwan has more than 540 recorded bird species, and the riverbank is one of the easiest places to start. Keen birders can expect a long list in a single morning.

Walks stay outside the core park on the buffer zone bank, but wild animals cross freely, so go with a guide. Rhinos and spotted deer often appear on the opposite bank in the first hour of light. Carry binoculars, wear neutral colours and keep your voice low. Walks take two to three hours and end before the heat of the day.

faqs.q: How many bird species are there in Chitwan?
faqs.a: Bird surveys in 2006 recorded 543 species in Chitwan National Park, more than in any other protected area in Nepal. About 160 migrant and vagrant species arrive in autumn to spend the winter, so November to March is the richest season for birding along the rivers and lakes.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide for a riverbank bird walk near Kasara?
faqs.a: We strongly recommend one. Even outside the park boundary, rhinos, sloth bears, wild elephants and crocodiles move along the river. A local bird guide knows the safe stretches, finds birds by call and helps with identification. Inside the park itself, a licensed guide is required.

faqs.q: What binoculars should I bring for birding in Chitwan?
faqs.a: An 8x42 or 10x42 pair works well for both river and forest birding. Lodges and guides sometimes lend binoculars, but quality varies, so bring your own if you can. A field guide to the birds of Nepal or a bird app with offline maps adds a lot.

experiences.title: Cycling the farm villages of Patihani
experiences.summary: Ride flat village tracks through rice and mustard fields, past Tharu and hill-settler homes, buffalo sheds and community forests in the buffer zone across the Rapti from Kasara, ending at the river for sunset. Bikes are provided by lodges.
body: Patihani is a farm area, and the best way to see it is on a bicycle. Tracks are flat and mostly unpaved, running between rice paddies in autumn and yellow mustard in winter. You pass houses built of mud and reed beside newer concrete homes, and courtyards where grain is spread to dry. Children wave from doorways and farmers stop to chat.

Along the way you meet the buffer zone in practice: community forests managed by local user groups, electric fences and trenches built to keep rhinos and elephants out of crops, and small temples at village crossroads. Your guide can explain how the park shares revenue with these communities and the cost of living beside wild animals. Ask about the crops in season.

Time the ride to end at the Rapti in the late afternoon. As the light drops, rhinos and deer often come to the far bank, and egrets fly to roost. Lodges provide bicycles and helmets; ask for one with gears if you want an easier ride. Rides cover 10 to 15 km on flat ground and suit most ages and fitness levels.

faqs.q: Is cycling safe around Chitwan's villages?
faqs.a: On the village tracks of the buffer zone, yes, with a local guide. Roads are flat and traffic light, but watch for motorbikes and tractors. Wild animals sometimes wander into fields, especially at dusk, so follow your guide and do not ride into forest areas alone or after dark.

faqs.q: Do I need to be fit to cycle in Patihani?
faqs.a: No. The terrain is flat and the pace relaxed, with stops to look at farms, forests and the river. Most rides cover 10 to 15 km in two to three hours. The main challenges are heat in spring and dust on dry tracks, so carry water and a scarf.

faqs.q: What will I see on a Chitwan village bike ride?
faqs.a: Expect rice, maize and mustard fields depending on season, traditional mud-and-reed houses next to new concrete ones, buffaloes and goats, community forests, village temples and the Rapti riverbank. If you are lucky, rhinos or deer on the far bank of the river at sunset.

faqs.q: What is Kasara in Chitwan?
faqs.a: Kasara is the headquarters of Chitwan National Park, on the south bank of the East Rapti in the middle of the park. It houses the park office, a small museum, an army post and the gharial breeding centre, where eggs of this critically endangered crocodile are hatched and the young raised for release into the rivers.

faqs.q: How far is Kasara from Sauraha?
faqs.a: About 35 km by road via Bharatpur and Patihani, which takes 1 to 1.5 hours. Most visitors reach Kasara on a full-day jeep safari through the park from Sauraha, which includes a lunch stop and a visit to the breeding centre before returning by a different track.

faqs.q: Can I stay overnight at Kasara?
faqs.a: There are no tourist rooms inside the park headquarters. The nearest stays are at Patihani across the Rapti, including Kasara Resort on the edge of the park. Bharatpur, about 40 minutes away, has more hotels. Staying at Patihani gives quieter access to the central part of the park.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee for the gharial breeding centre?
faqs.a: The centre lies inside the park, so you need a valid park entry permit for the day, which your lodge or guide arranges. Ask your guide whether a separate ticket applies this season. Fees change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Kasara?
faqs.a: October to April. February to April is best for wildlife on the drive in, and winter mornings are cool and pleasant at the breeding centre. In the monsoon, from mid-June to September, park roads may be closed and the river crossings difficult, so access to Kasara is limited.

faqs.q: Is Kasara good for children?
faqs.a: Yes. Children usually love seeing gharials of every size, from tiny hatchlings to large juveniles, and the turtle pens. The visit is short and easy. A full-day jeep drive to reach Kasara can be long for small children, so families often drive by road via Patihani instead.

faqs.q: Where can I see wild gharials in Chitwan?
faqs.a: Wild gharials live mainly in the Narayani River, along the park's western edge near Meghauli and Amaltari, and in deeper stretches of the Rapti. Canoe trips and riverbank walks in these areas give the best chance. Sightings are not guaranteed because numbers remain small.

faqs.q: What else is near Kasara?
faqs.a: Patihani across the river has farm villages and quiet riverbanks for birding. Bishazari Tal, the Ramsar-listed lake system, is about 30 to 40 minutes away near Bharatpur. Meghauli and its lodges lie further west. Sauraha is about 1 to 1.5 hours by road.

faqs.q: How old are the gharials when they are released?
faqs.a: Young gharials at the Kasara breeding centre are usually reared for six to nine years before release, when they are large enough to survive floods, predators and fishing nets. Releases take place in the Narayani, Rapti and other Terai rivers, and some released animals have been recorded far downstream.
